claims.text: Increasing vanadium content to 5 at.% in refractory W–Ta alloys will enhance radiation tolerance.
Increasing vanadium content to 5 at.% will preserve mechanical integrity.
A 5 at.% V addition promotes a more homogeneous BCC solid solution.
A 5 at.% V addition refines the nanocrystalline morphology.
The proposed homogeneous, refined nanocrystalline morphology improves defect recombination.
The proposed microstructural changes minimize irradiation-induced segregation and void formation.
The baseline materials are approximately 70 nm thick, magnetron-sputtered nanocrystalline BCC W–Ta films with equiaxed grains below 100 nm.
At 5 at.% V, Ta–V and W–V chemical short-range order leads to a more homogeneous BCC solid solution.
Vanadium-dependent chemical short-range order induces grain refinement.
The more homogeneous BCC structure and grain refinement modulate vacancy and self-interstitial populations.
Increased vanadium content lowers self-interstitial mobility relative to the W–Ta matrix.
Increased vanadium content makes vacancy and self-interstitial mobilities more similar.
More closely matched vacancy and self-interstitial mobilities enhance defect recombination.
Higher vanadium content weakens ordering or segregation tendencies.
Weakening segregation tendencies reduces irradiation-induced W enrichment and Ta depletion at grain boundaries.
Higher vanadium content limits the formation of large voids or interstitial clusters.
W53Ta42V5 will exhibit fewer and smaller voids than W44Ta56 and W53Ta44V3 after the specified irradiation.
W53Ta42V5 will exhibit less grain-boundary elemental segregation than W44Ta56 and W53Ta44V3 after the specified irradiation.
W53Ta42V5 will retain the nanocrystalline BCC morphology more effectively than W44Ta56 and W53Ta44V3 under the specified irradiation.
The predicted effect is scoped to approximately 70 nm sputtered films irradiated with 1 MeV Kr ions to about 20 dpa at 1073 K after annealing for 10 minutes at 1173 K.
